script.opening: "Hiya — I keep getting these water infections, I think I've got another one. Bit of pain low down in my tummy and some discharge. Could you just put me a prescription through for some antibiotics like last time? I'm at work, I don't really want a big fuss or to come in for tests and all that. It's just a UTI, isn't it?"

facts.text: If asked: low down on both sides of your tummy, a dull dragging ache, for about five days and slowly getting worse. 5/10. Not sudden, not one-sided.
Yellowish discharge that smells "a bit off", for about a week. Some spotting between periods and after sex.
Deep pain during sex, "right up inside". New boyfriend for three months; you use condoms "sometimes". No other partners in the last 6 months. You think he might have been seeing someone else.
A bit of stinging "when it touches" but no frequency or urgency. You have had two UTIs in the past year, diagnosed over the phone.
Felt hot and shivery last night; you have not taken your temperature. Eating, drinking and passing urine. No vomiting.
Last period three weeks ago, normal. No contraception except condoms sometimes. "I don't think I'm pregnant." No shoulder-tip pain, no fainting, no one-sided sharp pain. Happy to do a test.
23, works in a phone shop. Lives with a friend. Smokes 5 a day, drinks at weekends.

You are frightened it is an STI and embarrassed to say so. You are dreading having to raise it with your boyfriend. Quietly you wonder whether this could stop you having children one day. Reveal only if the doctor is non-judgemental and asks what you are worried about.

Chatty but in a hurry, keen to keep it to "a UTI". If questions about sex feel judgemental, get short and vague. If the doctor explains why they are asking and normalises it, answer honestly. You accept a pregnancy test, swabs and treatment if it is explained that treating now protects your fertility.

ice.concerns: Underneath: "What if it's something he's given me?" — and whether it could affect having children.
ice.expectations: "Can you just send antibiotics through like last time?" You will accept tests and proper treatment if you are not made to feel judged.

cues: "It's just a UTI, isn't it?" — say in the opening.
"It hurts when we... you know." — say hesitantly if asked about pain with sex.
"Could this stop me having kids?" — ask near the end if trust has been built.

checkpoints.text: Recognises PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE from the picture (bilateral lower abdominal pain, abnormal discharge, deep dyspareunia, IMB/PCB, fever, sexual risk) and does NOT treat it as a UTI with a quick antibiotic for cystitis

Excludes PREGNANCY/ECTOPIC: arranges a pregnancy test and screens the ectopic red flags (severe/unilateral pain, shoulder-tip pain, syncope, amenorrhoea), recognising abdominal pain in a young woman always needs this

Treats PID PROMPTLY and EMPIRICALLY (low threshold): starts recommended empirical antibiotic therapy (BASHH 2019 outpatient regimen: ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose, plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days) without waiting for swab results — because delay risks infertility, chronic pain and ectopic — while taking swabs (NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea) and arranging examination

Offers a full sexual-health assessment/screen (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV, syphilis), advice on abstaining until treated, contraception review, and considers sexual-health-clinic involvement — rather than a phone antibiotic alone

Handles PARTNER NOTIFICATION/contact tracing: explains current and recent partners (BASHH 2019: those from the previous 6 months) need testing/treatment to prevent reinfection and onward spread, offered supportively and confidentially (clinic/provider options), without shame
Hears the avoidance/shame and the fear of infidelity/judgement, surfaces it gently, and does NOT collude with "just a UTI"; normalises the situation and reduces stigma
Addresses the unspoken FERTILITY fear honestly: prompt treatment protects future fertility — which is exactly why acting now matters — with reassurance balanced by honesty

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags that mean urgent/emergency review (severe pain, high fever, vomiting, pregnancy/ectopic features → same-day/A&E), treatment plan and review at 72 hours (BASHH 2019) to confirm response, then results, partner-notification support, and documentation

worked.txt: "I’m glad you rang — but I don’t think this is a water infection, and I don’t want to just send the wrong antibiotic. Pain low down on both sides, the discharge, pain deep during sex, a bit of bleeding — that points to an infection higher up, in the womb and tubes, which we call PID. It’s common, it’s treatable, but it’s a different thing from a UTI and it matters that we get it right."

"First, an important check: any chance you could be pregnant? I ask everyone with tummy pain, because we always need to rule out a pregnancy in the wrong place. Any severe one-sided pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, or feeling faint? … Good. We’ll still do a pregnancy test to be sure."

"Here’s why I want to act quickly rather than wait for tests: with this kind of infection, treating promptly protects you — left too long it can affect the tubes and your fertility down the line. So I’d start you on antibiotics today, take some swabs at the same time, and arrange to examine you — not wait around for results first."

"Can I gently ask — is part of you worried this might be something caught from a partner? … You’re not in any trouble, and there’s no judgement here at all. It’s really common, and the kind thing to do for yourself is just to test for everything and treat it. We can check for the common infections including HIV, all confidentially."

"One part that feels awkward but really matters: your recent partner (or partners) would need testing and treating too — otherwise it can bounce straight back to you. The sexual-health clinic can even do that anonymously on your behalf if telling them yourself feels too hard. You don’t have to do that part alone."

"On the worry I suspect is underneath — your fertility — the honest, reassuring thing is that treating this promptly is exactly how we protect it, and most women who are treated quickly go on to have completely normal pregnancies. If meanwhile the pain becomes severe, you get a high fever, vomiting, or any of those one-sided/shoulder-tip pains — that’s same-day, go to A&E. I’ll start the treatment, sort the tests, and follow up your results with you."

f.learning: Bilateral lower abdominal pain with abnormal discharge, deep dyspareunia and intermenstrual/post-coital bleeding in a sexually-active young woman is pelvic inflammatory disease, NOT a UTI — and the cardinal rules are: always exclude pregnancy/ectopic (pregnancy test + red-flag screen), and treat PID PROMPTLY and EMPIRICALLY with a low threshold (BASHH 2019 outpatient regimen: ceftriaxone 1 g IM once, plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days), taking swabs/NAAT but NOT waiting for results, because delay risks tubal damage, chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy and infertility. Offer a full STI screen (incl. HIV), abstinence until treated, and contraception review. The examinable hidden agenda is shame/avoidance — she suspects a sexually transmitted cause, fears judgement and infidelity, dreads partner notification, and carries an unspoken fertility fear. Surface it gently without colluding with the "just a UTI" label, normalise and de-stigmatise, handle partner notification/contact tracing supportively (clinic/provider options), and address fertility honestly — prompt treatment protects it. Safety-net the PID/ectopic red flags.

knowledge.guideline: BASHH UK national guideline for the management of pelvic inflammatory disease (2018, 2019 update) · BASHH statement on partner notification (2012) · NICE NG253 (Sepsis, 16 and over) · GMC Confidentiality (2017)
knowledge.summary: Bilateral lower abdominal pain, abnormal discharge, deep dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding and fever in a 23-year-old with a new partner is pelvic inflammatory disease until proven otherwise. Exclude pregnancy, examine, take swabs and start treatment the same day.

points.t: BASHH 2019: lower abdominal pain, usually bilateral, with deep dyspareunia, abnormal vaginal or cervical discharge, intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, and fever. Cervical motion and adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination support it. Cystitis does not cause discharge or deep dyspareunia.

A pregnancy test is needed in every woman of reproductive age with pelvic pain, to exclude ectopic pregnancy and because doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy (BNF). Ask about one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or fainting.

BASHH 2019 advises a low threshold for empirical treatment because delay increases the risk of tubal damage, infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain. Outpatient regimen: ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose, plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days.

NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, plus HIV and syphilis testing. Results guide later changes but should not delay treatment. Review at 72 hours is recommended, especially with moderate or severe signs; no improvement needs further assessment.

Surgical emergency not excluded (ectopic, appendicitis), severe illness, suspected tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, inability to take oral treatment, or no response to outpatient treatment. Assess sepsis risk if she is systemically unwell (NICE NG253).

BASHH 2019: contact and test partners from the previous 6 months. Advise no sex until she and her partner(s) have completed treatment. Sexual health services can notify partners anonymously (BASHH 2012).

dg.d: Checked privacy at work; let her give her own explanation before testing it.
Worked around her being at work, her new relationship and her reluctance to attend.
Same-day pregnancy test, abdominal and bimanual examination, NAAT swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, HIV and syphilis tests.
PID versus UTI; ectopic pregnancy; appendicitis; features that would mean admission.
Screened ectopic red flags and pregnancy; checked for severe illness; clear A&E triggers.
Named PID in plain words and explained why a UTI antibiotic would be wrong.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: BASHH 2019 outpatient regimen started the same day after a negative pregnancy test; abstinence; partner notification with anonymous option.
Contraception discussed; fever and systemic features kept under review.
Teach-back, specific A&E red flags, a call at 72 hours and results follow-up.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

ro.d: Picked up “not always used condoms”, hesitation about sex and “not sure I’m the only one”, and explored them.
Idea (another UTI); concern (an STI, her fertility, telling her partner); expectation (antibiotics by phone, no tests).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Underneath: "What if it's something he's given me?" — and whether it could affect having children — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi, is that Demi Carter? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I just check your date of birth — and are you somewhere you can talk privately?
model.why: Checks identity and privacy before a sensitive telephone conversation

model.text: Yeah, I’ve stepped out of work. I think I’ve got another water infection — pain low down and some discharge. Can you just put the antibiotics through like last time? I don’t want a fuss.
I’ll help you get sorted today. To make sure the antibiotic is the right one, can I ask a few quick questions first? Then we’ll agree what to do.
model.why: Agrees to help while keeping space to assess

model.text: Fine, but quick if that’s okay.
Tell me about the pain — where is it, and how long has it been going on?
model.why: Open question about the main symptom

model.text: A few days. Low down, both sides. Achy.
Any burning when you pass urine, or going more often than usual?
Not really, no. It’s more the tummy and the discharge.
Has the pain been there during sex at all — especially deep inside?
(Pause.) Yeah, actually. That’s been sore.
Thank you for telling me. Any bleeding between periods or after sex, and have you felt hot or feverish?
model.why: Asks about abnormal bleeding and fever

model.text: A bit of spotting after sex. And I’ve felt a bit hot and shivery.
When was your last period, and could you possibly be pregnant? Any sharp pain on one side, pain in your shoulder tip, or feeling faint?
About three weeks ago. I’m not on anything. No, none of those.

I don’t think this is a water infection, Demi. Pain on both sides, discharge, pain deep during sex and some bleeding points to an infection higher up, in the womb and tubes. Can I ask — has anything been on your mind about what it might be?
model.why: Shares the thinking early and opens the door to her worry

model.text: (Long pause.) Is it… something I’ve caught? I’ve got a new partner. We’ve not always used condoms. And I’m not sure I’m the only one he’s seeing.
Thank you for trusting me with that — it can’t be easy to say at work. You’re not in any trouble, and there’s no judgement from me. Infections like this are common. What worries you most about it?
Whether it’ll mess me up. For having kids, I mean. And having to tell him.

This is called pelvic inflammatory disease, or PID. It’s often caused by infections like chlamydia or gonorrhoea, but not always. The reason I don’t want to just send a UTI antibiotic is that PID needs a different treatment, and treating it quickly is exactly what protects your fertility.
model.why: Names PID and links prompt treatment to her fertility concern

model.text: So it could affect having kids?
Left untreated, it can damage the tubes. Treated promptly, most women recover fully. That’s why I’d like to start treatment today rather than wait for results.
model.why: Honest about risk, balanced with reassurance

model.text: Okay. What do I need to do?

I need to see you today — could you come in at lunchtime or after work? We’ll do a pregnancy test, examine you gently, and take swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. I’d also recommend blood tests for HIV and syphilis — we test everyone, it’s routine. Then you’d have an injection and two courses of tablets for two weeks.
model.why: Same-day assessment, pregnancy test, swabs, full STI screen and BASHH regimen

model.text: Can I get there for half five?

Yes, I’ll book that now. No sex until you and your partner have both finished treatment. And any partners from the last six months need testing and treating too, otherwise it can come straight back. If telling him feels too hard, the sexual health clinic can contact him anonymously for you.
model.why: Abstinence and partner notification with a supportive option

model.text: Anonymously? That would help, honestly.
And while you’re in, we can talk about contraception so you’ve got something that suits you.
Before 5:30, if the pain becomes severe or one-sided, you get shoulder-tip pain, feel faint, start vomiting or feel really unwell and shivery, go straight to A&E. Can you tell me the plan back?
model.why: Specific red flags with a clear action, then teach-back

model.text: Come in at half five, pregnancy test and swabs, injection and tablets, no sex till we’re both treated, clinic can tell him. A&E if it gets bad.
Perfect. I’ll call you in three days to check you’re improving and go through the results. You did the right thing ringing.
model.why: Review at 72 hours and closes supportively

model.text: Thanks. I’m glad I didn’t just get the UTI tablets.

social.t: She is calling from work and wants to avoid attending. Offer a time that fits, so the barrier doesn’t become a reason to skip examination.
A new partner she may not trust. Explore whether she feels safe in the relationship if cues arise, without assuming.

legal.t: Sexual health information is confidential. Partner notification is done with her consent and can be anonymous through sexual health services (GMC Confidentiality 2017; BASHH 2012).

professional.t: Prescribing a UTI antibiotic by phone without examination or a pregnancy test in this presentation would be unsafe. Arrange face-to-face assessment the same day.
Stigma about STIs delays care. Test everyone routinely and say so (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: treat patients with respect and without discrimination).

community.t: Local sexual health clinic for testing, partner notification and contraception; many offer online STI testing kits.

redFlags: One-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or fainting — possible ectopic pregnancy
Severe pain, vomiting, high fever or feeling very unwell — needs hospital assessment
Pregnancy — changes treatment and needs specialist input
psychosocial: Calling from work, wants it quick
New partner, inconsistent condoms, worried he is seeing someone else
Shame about a possible STI and fear of telling him
ice: Concern: an STI from her partner; future fertility; the partner conversation
Expectation: antibiotics by phone without tests

playbook.diagnosis: Be clear: “I don’t think this is a water infection. Pain on both sides, discharge, pain deep during sex and bleeding after sex point to pelvic inflammatory disease — an infection of the womb and tubes.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A water infection is in the bladder, at the front. This is an infection that has travelled up through the neck of the womb into the womb and tubes. It needs different antibiotics, and quickly, to protect the tubes.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about having children one day. Treating this quickly is exactly how we protect that.”
management.psychosocial: Fit the appointment around work; normalise STI testing; offer anonymous partner notification so she doesn’t have to face that alone.
sharedPlan: Same-day: pregnancy test, examination, NAAT swabs, HIV and syphilis tests
BASHH 2019 regimen: ceftriaxone 1 g IM once, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days
No sex until she and partner(s) are treated; partners from last 6 months tested; contraception discussed
safetyNet: Severe or one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting, vomiting or feeling very unwell — A&E

pitfalls.intro: The patient hands you a diagnosis and a prescription. The station is failed by candidates who accept both, and by those who find PID but never find out why she is so keen to keep it quick.

items.fail: Prescribing nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim over the phone.
items.why: “Does not recognise the likely diagnosis.” No dysuria, plus discharge and deep dyspareunia, is not cystitis.
items.fix: Ask about urinary symptoms, deep pain with sex, bleeding and fever before accepting the label.

items.why: Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded, and doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
items.fix: Last period, contraception, one-sided or shoulder-tip pain, fainting — and a test the same day.

items.fail: Waiting for swab results before treating.
items.why: BASHH 2019 advises empirical treatment on clinical suspicion because delay risks infertility.
items.fix: Swabs and treatment at the same visit.

items.fail: Asking about sexual partners in a clipped, checklist way.
items.why: “Does not put the patient at ease.” Shame will close her down.
items.fix: Check privacy first, then normalise: “We ask everyone, and it’s all confidential.”

items.why: It is the concern underneath; naming it turns her from reluctant to engaged.
items.fix: “What worries you most about it?” Then link prompt treatment to protecting fertility.

items.fail: No partner plan and a vague safety-net.
items.why: Reinfection is likely without partner treatment; non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Partners from the last 6 months, anonymous notification, no sex until both treated; named A&E red flags; 72-hour review.

timeMap.d: She is at work. Check she can talk before asking about sex.
No urinary symptoms. Ask directly: deep pain with sex, bleeding, fever, last period, pregnancy and ectopic red flags.
Share that this isn’t a UTI and ask what she’s been thinking. The partner, the STI fear and fertility come out.
PID in plain words. Prompt treatment protects fertility.
Same-day visit: pregnancy test, examination, swabs, BASHH regimen. Partners from the last 6 months, no sex until treated. A&E red flags. Call at 72 hours.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a UTI antibiotic by phone; no pregnancy test; no sexual history; or lectures about condoms; waits for swab results before treating; no partner notification; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises PID, arranges a pregnancy test and examination, takes swabs, starts appropriate antibiotics, mentions partner treatment and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: draws out the worry about the partner without judgement; links prompt treatment to her fertility fear; full STI screen framed as routine; anonymous partner notification offered; abstinence and 6-month look-back explained; ectopic red flags with A&E; teach-back and 72-hour review.

avoid.dont: "You should really be using condoms with a new partner."
avoid.instead: "You’re not in any trouble. Infections like this are common, and the important thing is getting you treated."
avoid.why: Judgement shuts down disclosure; she is already ashamed.

avoid.dont: "I’ll wait for the swab results and then decide on antibiotics."
avoid.instead: "I’d like to start treatment today, while we wait for the results."
avoid.why: BASHH advises a low threshold for empirical treatment; delay risks tubal damage.

avoid.dont: "You’ll need to tell your partner he has an STI."
avoid.instead: "Your partner needs testing too. If telling him feels too hard, the clinic can contact him anonymously."
avoid.why: An anonymous option makes partner notification more likely to happen.

NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, plus HIV and syphilis testing. Results guide later changes but should not delay treatment. Review at 72 hours is recommended, especially with moderate or severe signs; no improvement needs further assessment.

Surgical emergency not excluded (ectopic, appendicitis), severe illness, suspected tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, inability to take oral treatment, or no response to outpatient treatment. Assess sepsis risk if she is systemically unwell (NICE NG253).

BASHH 2019: contact and test partners from the previous 6 months. Advise no sex until she and her partner(s) have completed treatment. Sexual health services can notify partners anonymously (BASHH 2012).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked privacy at work; let her give her own explanation before testing it.
Worked around her being at work, her new relationship and her reluctance to attend.
Picked up “not always used condoms”, hesitation about sex and “not sure I’m the only one”, and explored them.
Idea (another UTI); concern (an STI, her fertility, telling her partner); expectation (antibiotics by phone, no tests).
Same-day pregnancy test, abdominal and bimanual examination, NAAT swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, HIV and syphilis tests.
PID versus UTI; ectopic pregnancy; appendicitis; features that would mean admission.
Screened ectopic red flags and pregnancy; checked for severe illness; clear A&E triggers.
Named PID in plain words and explained why a UTI antibiotic would be wrong.
BASHH 2019 outpatient regimen started the same day after a negative pregnancy test; abstinence; partner notification with anonymous option.
Contraception discussed; fever and systemic features kept under review.
Teach-back, specific A&E red flags, a call at 72 hours and results follow-up.

social.t: She is calling from work and wants to avoid attending. Offer a time that fits, so the barrier doesn’t become a reason to skip examination.
A new partner she may not trust. Explore whether she feels safe in the relationship if cues arise, without assuming.

legal.t: Sexual health information is confidential. Partner notification is done with her consent and can be anonymous through sexual health services (GMC Confidentiality 2017; BASHH 2012).

professional.t: Prescribing a UTI antibiotic by phone without examination or a pregnancy test in this presentation would be unsafe. Arrange face-to-face assessment the same day.
Stigma about STIs delays care. Test everyone routinely and say so (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: treat patients with respect and without discrimination).

community.t: Local sexual health clinic for testing, partner notification and contraception; many offer online STI testing kits.

redFlags: One-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or fainting — possible ectopic pregnancy
Severe pain, vomiting, high fever or feeling very unwell — needs hospital assessment
Pregnancy — changes treatment and needs specialist input

New partner, inconsistent condoms, worried he is seeing someone else
Shame about a possible STI and fear of telling him
ice: Concern: an STI from her partner; future fertility; the partner conversation
Expectation: antibiotics by phone without tests

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be clear: “I don’t think this is a water infection. Pain on both sides, discharge, pain deep during sex and bleeding after sex point to pelvic inflammatory disease — an infection of the womb and tubes.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A water infection is in the bladder, at the front. This is an infection that has travelled up through the neck of the womb into the womb and tubes. It needs different antibiotics, and quickly, to protect the tubes.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about having children one day. Treating this quickly is exactly how we protect that.”
management.psychosocial: Fit the appointment around work; normalise STI testing; offer anonymous partner notification so she doesn’t have to face that alone.
sharedPlan: Same-day: pregnancy test, examination, NAAT swabs, HIV and syphilis tests

No sex until she and partner(s) are treated; partners from last 6 months tested; contraception discussed
safetyNet: Severe or one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting, vomiting or feeling very unwell — A&E

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The patient hands you a diagnosis and a prescription. The station is failed by candidates who accept both, and by those who find PID but never find out why she is so keen to keep it quick.

items.fail: Prescribing nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim over the phone.
items.why: “Does not recognise the likely diagnosis.” No dysuria, plus discharge and deep dyspareunia, is not cystitis.
items.fix: Ask about urinary symptoms, deep pain with sex, bleeding and fever before accepting the label.

items.why: Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded, and doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
items.fix: Last period, contraception, one-sided or shoulder-tip pain, fainting — and a test the same day.

items.fail: Waiting for swab results before treating.
items.why: BASHH 2019 advises empirical treatment on clinical suspicion because delay risks infertility.
items.fix: Swabs and treatment at the same visit.

items.fail: Asking about sexual partners in a clipped, checklist way.
items.why: “Does not put the patient at ease.” Shame will close her down.
items.fix: Check privacy first, then normalise: “We ask everyone, and it’s all confidential.”

items.why: It is the concern underneath; naming it turns her from reluctant to engaged.
items.fix: “What worries you most about it?” Then link prompt treatment to protecting fertility.

items.fail: No partner plan and a vague safety-net.
items.why: Reinfection is likely without partner treatment; non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Partners from the last 6 months, anonymous notification, no sex until both treated; named A&E red flags; 72-hour review.
